# dtcloud_volume (Resource)

Manages a block storage volume.

This resource owns the volume itself: creating it, renaming it, growing it and changing its storage
policy. Attaching it to a machine is a separate resource, `dtcloud_vm_volume_attachment`. A disk a
machine boots from is not a `dtcloud_volume`: it comes from the `block_device` block on
`dtcloud_vm`.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# A blank data disk.
resource "dtcloud_volume" "data" {
  name           = "app-data"
  size           = 100
  storage_policy = data.dtcloud_storage_policies.available.policies[0].name
}

# A volume seeded from an image. The source is fixed at create time: changing it
# replaces the volume.
resource "dtcloud_volume" "boot" {
  name           = "web-01-boot"
  size           = 40
  storage_policy = "standard"
  image_id       = var.image_id
}
```

-> `image_id`, `source_volume_id` and `source_snapshot_id` are mutually exclusive: set one to seed
the volume's contents, or none for a blank volume.

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the volume. Can be changed in place.
- `size` (Number) Size in GB, between 1 and 8192. Can be grown in place; shrinking is impossible and is refused when applied.
- `storage_policy` (String) Name of the storage policy backing the volume, as listed by the dtcloud_storage_policies data source. Changing it retypes the volume in place.

### Optional

- `description` (String) Free-text description. Write-only: the API accepts it but never reports it back, so it does not drift, does not survive import, and cannot be cleared.
- `image_id` (String) Create the volume from this image, making it bootable. Changing it recreates the volume.
- `source_snapshot_id` (String) Restore the volume from this snapshot. `size` must be at least the snapshot's size. Changing it recreates the volume.
- `source_volume_id` (String) Create the volume as a clone of this one. Changing it recreates the volume.
- `timeouts` (Block, Optional) (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--timeouts))

### Read-Only

- `attached_to` (String) Name of the VM this volume is attached to, empty when detached.
- `attached_to_id` (String) ID of the VM this volume is attached to, empty when detached.
- `attached_to_status` (String) Status of the VM this volume is attached to.
- `bootable` (Boolean) Whether the volume can be booted from. True for volumes built from an image.
- `created` (String) When the volume was created, as reported by the platform.
- `id` (String) The ID of this resource.
- `image_metadata` (List of Object) Details of the image this volume was created from. Empty for a blank volume. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--image_metadata))
- `is_detachable` (Boolean) Whether the platform will allow this volume to be detached.
- `last_modified` (String) When the volume last changed, as reported by the platform.
- `status` (String) Status reported by the platform, e.g. available or in-use.
- `volume_type` (String) HDD, or CD-ROM when the volume holds an ISO. Derived by the platform, not the storage policy.

## Behaviour worth knowing

~> **An attached volume cannot be deleted.** The platform refuses to delete a volume that is
`in-use`, so the provider checks first and names the machine it is attached to. It will not detach
the volume for you. When the attachment is a `dtcloud_vm_volume_attachment` that references this
volume, Terraform removes the attachment first on its own.

* **What changes in place.** `name`, `description`, `size` and `storage_policy`. The three sources
  force a new volume: they seed its contents at create time, and no endpoint seeds an existing one
  again.
* **`size` can only be grown.** A lower value is refused rather than turned into a replacement, which
  would destroy the data. It is refused at apply, not at plan, because a plan cannot tell a lowered
  number from a volume grown outside Terraform, and refusing at plan would also block
  `terraform destroy`. If a plan proposes to shrink a volume you did not edit, raise `size` to match.
* **`description` is write-only.** The API never reports it back, so it cannot drift, does not survive
  an import and cannot be cleared. It is applied by a second call after the volume is created.
* **Growing and retyping look finished before they are.** The volume stays `available` with its old
  size or policy for a while, so the provider waits for the value it asked for rather than for the
  status.
* **`storage_policy` is a name.** A volume created with a volume type id reads back as the name, and
  every later plan proposes a change. `dtcloud_storage_policies` lists the names.
* **Deleting takes the snapshots with it.** The delete cascades, so every snapshot of the volume goes
  too, including snapshots managed as `dtcloud_snapshot`, without a warning from Terraform. Check with
  `dtcloud_volume_snapshots` first. Snapshots that reference this volume in `volume_id` are destroyed
  before it.

## Timeouts

`create` and `update` each default to 30 minutes, `delete` to 20 minutes. All three are asynchronous,
and creating from an image or growing a large volume takes a while, so the defaults are generous.
Override them with a `timeouts` block:

```terraform
resource "dtcloud_volume" "data" {
  # ...

  timeouts {
    create = "1h"
  }
}
```

## Import

```shell
terraform import dtcloud_volume.data 8a4f2c15-6b93-4d0e-a7f1-2c5b8e9d3a66
```

`description`, `image_id`, `source_volume_id` and `source_snapshot_id` are not reported by the
details endpoint, so they are empty after an import. `image_metadata.image_id` is not a substitute:
it names the image the contents came from, which a clone or a restore inherits. The three sources
force a new volume, so if the configuration sets one, the first plan after an import proposes a
rebuild. Ignore it to keep the imported volume:

```terraform
resource "dtcloud_volume" "data" {
  # ...

  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [image_id, source_volume_id, source_snapshot_id]
  }
}
```
